title: The Evidential THRESHOLD for Resurrection Belief - Gary Habermas
summary: In this interview chapter, Gary Habermas clarifies his evidential threshold for historical claims about the resurrection. He refuses to assign a numerical probability threshold for 'highly evidenced,' instead relying on categories such as multiple attestation, eyewitness testimony, and early sources. He also clarifies that he has never counted scholarly consensus percentages except for the empty tomb, and that the first criterion (high evidence) is far more important than the second (scholarly consensus) for rational belief.

atoms.name: No numerical evidential threshold for historical facts
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas does not require a specific percentage of evidence for a historical fact to qualify as 'highly evidenced'; instead he uses qualitative categories such as multiple attestation, eyewitness testimony, and early sources.
atoms.statementPlain: There is no set number (like 51% or 80%) that evidence must reach for a historical fact to be believable; instead, strong categories of evidence matter more.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If Habermas were to state a specific numerical threshold (e.g., 'I require at least 80% evidence') in his published works or interviews, this claim would be falsified.
atoms.notes: Habermas explicitly refuses to give a number, citing misuse by critics.

atoms.name: Scholarly consensus percentages are not used except for the empty tomb
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas has never counted scholarly consensus percentages for the minimal facts, except for the empty tomb, and does not require a specific percentage (e.g., 90%) for a fact to qualify.
atoms.statementPlain: He doesn't use numbers like '90% of scholars agree' for most facts; the only time he counted was for the empty tomb.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If Habermas were to produce a published count showing he regularly uses percentage thresholds for the minimal facts, this claim would be falsified.
atoms.notes: He emphasizes that he reports where scholars are, not exact percentages.

atoms.name: Criterion 1 (high evidence) is far more important than criterion 2 (scholarly consensus)
atoms.statementTechnical: For rational belief in the resurrection, the first criterion (a fact being highly evidenced) is significantly more important than the second criterion (vast majority of scholars concurring).
atoms.statementPlain: Having strong evidence is much more important than having many scholars agree.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If Habermas were to state that scholarly consensus is equally or more important than evidence for rational belief, this claim would be falsified.
atoms.notes: He estimates criterion 1 is 85-90% of the game.

atoms.name: Multiple attestation, eyewitness, and early sources as strong evidence
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas cites multiple attestation, eyewitness testimony, and early creedal sources as the strongest categories of evidence for the resurrection.
atoms.statementPlain: The best evidence includes many independent sources, eyewitnesses, and early accounts.
atoms.notes: He mentions Jimmy Dunn and Bart Ehrman as non-evangelical scholars who support these categories.

atoms.name: Ancient historians reported supernatural events
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas argues that ancient historians like Herodotus, Tacitus, and Suetonius reported supernatural events, so dismissing the Gospels for containing miracles is inconsistent.
atoms.statementPlain: Other ancient historians wrote about miracles too, so you can't just dismiss the Gospels for having miracles.
atoms.notes: He challenges critics to check ancient sources before claiming historians don't report miracles.

atoms.name: Critics may misrepresent any numerical threshold
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas fears that if he gives a specific percentage threshold, critics will misquote him as requiring that percentage for all facts.
atoms.statementPlain: If he gives a number, people will twist it and say he requires that number for everything.
atoms.notes: This is his stated reason for avoiding numbers.

atoms.name: Interview context and personal remarks
atoms.notes: Includes personal anecdotes, mentions of Dale, Jimmy Dunn, Bart Ehrman, Gerd Lüdemann, and the setting of the interview.
